analysis.one_liner: Tightens executive pay rules at banks bailed out with taxpayer money.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Financial Services Committee and died when the 111th Congress ended, without a vote and without a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would direct the Treasury Secretary to impose strict pay and governance standards on any bank or financial institution receiving help under the Troubled Asset Relief Program, the 2008 bailout, for as long as that help is outstanding. Bailed-out institutions would have to strip out pay plans that reward excessive risk-taking, claw back bonuses based on inaccurate earnings, ban golden parachute severance packages, stop paying bonuses to their 25 highest-paid employees, and get rid of corporate jets. The Treasury Secretary could also send an observer to the company's board meetings. It would close a loophole so that the ban on golden parachutes applies to all government purchases of troubled assets, not just large ones.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers who funded the bank bailout, and bank shareholders, because executives at bailed-out institutions could no longer collect risk-heavy bonuses, golden parachute severance, or bonuses for their top 25 earners while taxpayer assistance was outstanding, and Treasury could watch board decisions directly.

how_it_helps.text: Bailed-out institutions would have to remove pay incentives that push senior executives to take unnecessary and excessive risks that threaten the company's value, for as long as government assistance is outstanding.

Institutions could not pay golden parachute severance packages to senior executives, could not pay any bonus or incentive compensation to their 25 most highly-paid employees, and would have to recover bonuses based on earnings statements later found to be materially inaccurate.

The bill bans compensation plans designed to manipulate reported earnings to inflate employee pay, bars bailed-out institutions from owning, leasing, or holding an interest in private passenger aircraft unless they commit to divest ones they already had, and lets the Treasury Secretary place an observer at board meetings.

It strikes the $300 million threshold in the 2008 bailout law so that all government auction purchases of troubled assets are covered by the prohibition on senior executive golden parachute contracts, not just purchases above $300 million per institution.

analysis.who_pays: Senior executives and top earners at banks that took bailout money: they would lose risk-inflated bonuses, golden parachutes, bonuses for the top 25 earners, and corporate jets while taxpayer assistance was outstanding, and the banks would lose some autonomy over board and pay decisions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Bailed-out bank executives and their top earners

drawbacks.text: The rules only apply while government assistance is outstanding, so a bank that repays TARP immediately escapes every one of the restrictions, and banks might rush to return the money to avoid them.

Blanket bans on bonuses for the 25 highest-paid employees and on aircraft could push compensation off the books or into other forms, and could make it harder for assisted institutions to keep or hire experienced executives, a cost honest supporters would acknowledge.
The bill reaches only TARP recipients rather than the financial sector as a whole, so risky pay practices at firms that never took bailout money would continue untouched.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is straightforward accountability: firms kept alive with taxpayer money should not pay their leaders big bonuses and golden parachutes while the public is on the hook. The main design weakness is that everything is tied to TARP money still being outstanding, so the restrictions lapse as soon as a bank repays, and the across-the-board bonus ban for the top 25 earners is blunt and easier to engineer around than risk-based pay rules. Still, the costs fall almost entirely on a small group of well-paid executives at rescued institutions, while the benefit is real protection for taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Representative Gabrielle Giffords introduced the bill on February 4, 2009, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no vote, and no further action of any kind after the referral to committee.
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and all bills not passed by then die automatically.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Senior executives and top earners at TARP-assisted banks came out ahead: no restrictions were imposed, so bonus pools, golden parachutes, and corporate perks connected to bailout money were never constrained by this bill, and their institutions avoided new Treasury oversight of their boards. Taxpayers got no additional protection beyond what the 2008 bailout law already required.

for.name: Rep. Gabrielle Giffords
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 4, 2009 to impose pay and governance standards on TARP-assisted institutions.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on February 4, 2009 and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it; the bill sat in committee until the Congress ended.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor at any point in the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors from either party, and it never reached a vote, so no party split was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Banks and financial institutions receiving TARP assistance
industries.note: The bill would strip risk-inflated bonuses, golden parachutes, top-25 bonus pools, and corporate jets from rescued institutions while taxpayer money was outstanding, and put a Treasury observer in their boardrooms. Their gain in keeping those practices is a direct cost to the taxpayers who funded the rescue.

industries.industry: Business jet manufacturers and aircraft lessors
industries.note: Bailed-out banks could no longer own, lease, or hold an interest in private passenger aircraft, removing some demand from the luxury aircraft market. The public benefit here is symbolic but the industry cost is real, though grandfathered aircraft could be kept if the institution showed it was divesting.
